figures.alt: A plane's Wi-Fi reaches the internet through a satellite and a ground station, shared by everyone on board

figures.caption: **Figure 1. One switch, three radios.** Keep cellular off in the air. Turn Wi-Fi and Bluetooth back on only if the airline allows it.
figures.alt: Airplane mode turns off cellular, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth; in the air, cellular stays off and Wi-Fi and Bluetooth may come back on

figures.caption: **Figure 2. Your phone remembers your last flight.** Left, last time: you turned Wi-Fi back on. Right, this time: airplane mode leaves it on.
figures.alt: Your phone remembers: if you turned Wi-Fi on last flight, airplane mode may leave it on next time

figures.caption: **Figure 3. What to look for.** Signal bars, or 5G or LTE next to the carrier name, mean cellular is still on.
figures.alt: Good: airplane symbol, no signal bars, no carrier name. Not yet: signal bars and a carrier name mean cellular is on

figures.caption: **Figure 4. A phone in the air sees too many towers.** On the ground, hills and buildings limit how many towers your phone reaches. Up high, nothing is in the way. Not to scale.
figures.alt: On the ground a phone reaches a few towers; up in the air it reaches many at once

figures.caption: **Figure 5. Three ways down to the ground.** Towers work over land. Satellites also work over oceans. The far-away satellite adds the most delay. Not to scale.
figures.alt: Three ways down: towers over land, a low close satellite, and a far-away satellite with the longest delay

figures.caption: **Figure 6. The long way round.** Your message and its reply each go up to the satellite and back down. Follow the numbers 1 to 4. Not to scale.
figures.alt: Your message goes up to a far-away satellite and down to the ground, and the reply makes the same trip back: four long trips

figures.caption: **Figure 7. Everyone on board shares the link.** The same link, cut into a few wide lanes at home and many thin slices on a plane. Not to scale.
figures.alt: At home a few people share the link in wide lanes; on a plane everyone on board shares one link in thin slices

figures.caption: **Figure 8. Small jobs fit in your slice. Big ones don't.** Each bar is how much of the link a job needs; the dashed line is your share. Not to scale.
figures.alt: Message apps and email fit inside your slice of the shared link; web pages are slower; video calls and big downloads need more than your slice

figures.caption: **Figure 9. How the sign-in page appears.** Your phone checks whether it's online. The plane's network answers with its sign-in page instead.
figures.alt: Join the plane's Wi-Fi; your phone asks for a test page; the plane answers with its sign-in page

figures.caption: **Figure 10. Open a browser; don't tap Cancel.** Left: going to any web page brings up the sign-in page. Right: on an iPhone, Cancel disconnects you.
figures.alt: If the sign-in page does not appear, open a browser and go to any page. On an iPhone, do not tap Cancel

figures.caption: **Figure 11. Do the heavy lifting on the ground.** Left, on a fast connection before you board. Right, on the shared link in the air.
figures.alt: Before you board, on a fast connection: download, pair earbuds, finish updates. In the air: check your screen and text instead of calling
